results.name: coherent_set_far_violation_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets more than 20 from every example that break the set's coincidence (wrong final digit for same-digit sets, else not a multiple of 5 for all-multiple-of-5 sets, else wrong parity for same-parity sets), among 2-4-example coherent sets; observed > null means the model's steepened slope drives these rejections too close to zero (people keep a residual yes floor), observed < null means the model accepts them too often.
results.code:
# name: coherent_set_far_violation_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets more than 20 from every example that break the set's coincidence (wrong final digit for same-digit sets, else not a multiple of 5 for all-multiple-of-5 sets, else wrong parity for same-parity sets), among 2-4-example coherent sets; observed > null means the model's steepened slope drives these rejections too close to zero (people keep a residual yes floor), observed < null means the model accepts them too often.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    par = s % 2
    same_par = (par.max(axis=1) == par.min(axis=1)).values
    dig = s % 10
    same_dig = (dig.max(axis=1) == dig.min(axis=1)).values
    f5 = ((s % 5 == 0) | s.isna()).all(axis=1).values
    e0 = s[0].values.astype(int)
    viol = np.where(same_dig, (t % 10) != (e0 % 10),
                    np.where(f5, (t % 5) != 0, (t % 2) != (e0 % 2)))
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(s.values - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & (same_par | same_dig | f5) & viol & (dmin > 20)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: single_example_cell_polarization
results.description: Among (set, target) cells from one-example sets, fraction of cells whose yes-rate is <=1/9 or >=8/9; observed > null means people answer all-or-none after a lone example even though the model (no coincidence, so its least-steep slope) predicts graded answers there; observed < null means the model is too polarized there.

results.name: incoherent_multi_cell_polarization
results.description: Among (set, target) cells from 2-4-example sets with no coincidence (examples differ in parity, are not all multiples of 5, and do not share a final digit), fraction of cells with yes-rate <=1/9 or >=8/9; observed > null means people are all-or-none even after incoherent multi-example sets (decisiveness not confined to coherent sets), observed < null means the model over-polarizes them.
results.code:
# name: incoherent_multi_cell_polarization
# description: Among (set, target) cells from 2-4-example sets with no coincidence (examples differ in parity, are not all multiples of 5, and do not share a final digit), fraction of cells with yes-rate <=1/9 or >=8/9; observed > null means people are all-or-none even after incoherent multi-example sets (decisiveness not confined to coherent sets), observed < null means the model over-polarizes them.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1)
    par = s % 2
    same_par = par.max(axis=1) == par.min(axis=1)
    dig = s % 10
    same_dig = dig.max(axis=1) == dig.min(axis=1)
    f5 = ((s % 5 == 0) | s.isna()).all(axis=1)
    inc = (n >= 2) & ~same_par & ~same_dig & ~f5
    d = df[inc.values]
    y = d.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].mean()
    if len(y) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(((y <= 1/9 + 1e-9) | (y >= 8/9 - 1e-9)).mean())

results.name: odd_example_multiple_parity_contrast
results.description: For one-example sets with an odd example e>1, yes-rate for odd multiples of e (t=k*e, k>1) minus yes-rate for even multiples of e; observed < null means the model's parity-switch cut on the multiples route is too strong (people accept even multiples like 14 after "7" nearly as often as odd ones), observed > null means the cut is too weak.
results.code:
# name: odd_example_multiple_parity_contrast
# description: For one-example sets with an odd example e>1, yes-rate for odd multiples of e (t=k*e, k>1) minus yes-rate for even multiples of e; observed < null means the model's parity-switch cut on the multiples route is too strong (people accept even multiples like 14 after "7" nearly as often as odd ones), observed > null means the cut is too weak.
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    e = pd.to_numeric(df["number_set"].str.split(",").str[0]).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].values
    base = (n.values == 1) & (e % 2 == 1) & (e > 1) & (t % e == 0) & (t != e)
    a = base & (t % 2 == 1)
    b = base & (t % 2 == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: coherent_polarization_set_size_contrast
results.description: Among cells from coherent sets (all same parity, all multiples of 5, or all same final digit), fraction of polarized cells (yes-rate <=1/9 or >=8/9) in 4-example sets minus that in 2-example sets; observed < null means the model's coincidence-driven decisiveness grows too fast with the number of examples (people are not more all-or-none after 4 coherent examples than after 2), observed > null means it grows too slowly.
results.code:
# name: coherent_polarization_set_size_contrast
# description: Among cells from coherent sets (all same parity, all multiples of 5, or all same final digit), fraction of polarized cells (yes-rate <=1/9 or >=8/9) in 4-example sets minus that in 2-example sets; observed < null means the model's coincidence-driven decisiveness grows too fast with the number of examples (people are not more all-or-none after 4 coherent examples than after 2), observed > null means it grows too slowly.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1)
    par = s % 2
    same_par = par.max(axis=1) == par.min(axis=1)
    dig = s % 10
    same_dig = dig.max(axis=1) == dig.min(axis=1)
    f5 = ((s % 5 == 0) | s.isna()).all(axis=1)
    coh = (n >= 2) & (same_par | same_dig | f5)
    d = df.assign(_n=n.values)[coh.values]
    g = d.groupby(["number_set", "target"]).agg(y=("rating", "mean"), k=("_n", "first"))
    pol = (g["y"] <= 1/9 + 1e-9) | (g["y"] >= 8/9 - 1e-9)
    a = pol[g["k"] == 4]
    b = pol[g["k"] == 2]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: parity_outlier_neighborhood_contrast
results.description: In 3-4-example sets where exactly one example differs in parity from the rest (e.g. 27 in "92,82,27,42"), yes-rate for targets within 10 of the outlier (and >10 from all other examples) minus yes-rate for targets within 10 of a majority example (and >10 from the outlier); observed < null means people discount the odd-one-out example more than the model's summed similarity does, observed > null means the model discounts it too much.
results.code:
# name: parity_outlier_neighborhood_contrast
# description: In 3-4-example sets where exactly one example differs in parity from the rest (e.g. 27 in "92,82,27,42"), yes-rate for targets within 10 of the outlier (and >10 from all other examples) minus yes-rate for targets within 10 of a majority example (and >10 from the outlier); observed < null means people discount the odd-one-out example more than the model's summed similarity does, observed > null means the model discounts it too much.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    v = s.values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    n = (~np.isnan(v)).sum(axis=1)
    p = np.where(np.isnan(v), np.nan, v % 2)
    odd = np.nansum(p, axis=1)
    out_par = np.where(odd == 1, 1.0, np.where(odd == n - 1, 0.0, np.nan))
    has = (n >= 3) & ~np.isnan(out_par)
    is_out = (p == out_par[:, None]) & has[:, None]
    d = np.abs(v - t[:, None])
    d_out = np.where(is_out, d, np.inf).min(axis=1)
    d_maj = np.where(~is_out & ~np.isnan(v), d, np.inf).min(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].values
    a = has & (d_out <= 10) & (d_maj > 10)
    b = has & (d_maj <= 10) & (d_out > 10)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
results.description: In 2-4-example sets, yes-rate for targets within 10 of the first-shown example (and >10 from the last) minus yes-rate for targets within 10 of the last-shown example (and >10 from the first); observed > null means people weight the first example more than the order-blind model (primacy), observed < null means a recency weighting.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
# description: In 2-4-example sets, yes-rate for targets within 10 of the first-shown example (and >10 from the last) minus yes-rate for targets within 10 of the last-shown example (and >10 from the first); observed > null means people weight the first example more than the order-blind model (primacy), observed < null means a recency weighting.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    v = s.values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    n = (~np.isnan(v)).sum(axis=1)
    first = v[:, 0]
    last = v[np.arange(len(v)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    df_ = np.abs(t - first)
    dl = np.abs(t - last)
    r = df["rating"].values
    a = (n >= 2) & (df_ <= 10) & (dl > 10)
    b = (n >= 2) & (dl <= 10) & (df_ > 10)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: coherent_far_consistent_set_size_slope
results.description: Among coherent 2-4-example sets (same final digit, all multiples of 5, or same parity), yes-rate for rule-consistent targets more than 20 from every example in 4-example sets minus in 2-example sets; observed > null means people extend the rule to far targets more with more examples than the model (whose averaging penalty and distance gradient dominate), observed < null means the model over-extends it with set size.
results.code:
# name: coherent_far_consistent_set_size_slope
# description: Among coherent 2-4-example sets (same final digit, all multiples of 5, or same parity), yes-rate for rule-consistent targets more than 20 from every example in 4-example sets minus in 2-example sets; observed > null means people extend the rule to far targets more with more examples than the model (whose averaging penalty and distance gradient dominate), observed < null means the model over-extends it with set size.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    par = s % 2
    same_par = (par.max(axis=1) == par.min(axis=1)).values
    dig = s % 10
    same_dig = (dig.max(axis=1) == dig.min(axis=1)).values
    f5 = ((s % 5 == 0) | s.isna()).all(axis=1).values
    e0 = s[0].values.astype(int)
    viol = np.where(same_dig, (t % 10) != (e0 % 10),
                    np.where(f5, (t % 5) != 0, (t % 2) != (e0 % 2)))
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(s.values - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    base = (same_par | same_dig | f5) & ~viol & (dmin > 20)
    r = df["rating"].values
    a = base & (n == 4)
    b = base & (n == 2)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
